text: Two riders crossing fields for a hundred and three minutes, and the talk between them is the event. Albert Serra puts Don Quixote and Sancho on the road in Catalan, riding day and night, letting the conversation go where it wants: chivalry, spirituality, the ordinary business of getting through an afternoon. What accumulates is not incident but company, hour by hour. The friendship is the plot, and it is assembled out of small talk and waiting. Slowness gets declared in the first minutes rather than sprung later, so the film sorts its audience honestly and early. Somewhere in the middle the two of them become each other's habit, which is a stranger and warmer thing than any adventure the pair set out to find.

In 1976 a Spanish family agreed to sit in front of a camera and talk about their dead father. He was the poet Leopoldo Panero; the speakers are his widow and his sons, and Jaime Chávarri's film is built almost entirely out of what they prove willing to say in front of one another. Death is the announced subject, taken generally at first. It narrows fast, into the affairs of one house and what those arrangements cost the people inside them. Ninety-seven minutes is time enough for the equipment to be forgotten, and that forgetting is the whole gamble. What the camera catches is not grief so much as a family still doing what a family does, now with witnesses, and with a poet's reputation sitting in the room.

A middle-aged man watches a dancer who also sells herself, and the watching is where the film lives. Bigas Luna keeps close to him for ninety-three minutes, near enough that a routine begins to look like a system: hours arranged around one person, a life organised down to its smallest detail by a single fixation. That proximity is the method and the risk, since obsession filmed from inside is not the same thing as obsession explained. The genre labels read drama and thriller, and both are accurate in the flattest way — the dread is domestic, made of repetition, and it is present long before anything is done. Spain, 1978. The film is uncomfortable by design and exact about the discomfort, which is the difference between a hard film and a cheap one.

A film made in 1997 that keeps quiet, as if sound had never arrived, and turns on a French photographer who went missing in the 1920s. José Luis Guerín rebuilds that disappearance instead of reporting it: the footage looks found, the film behaves like something recovered from a cupboard, and the exercise is an homage to cinema's first years, when a strip of exposed celluloid was itself the news. Caimán's hundred-best survey of Spanish film found room for it, which for a silent experiment finished at the end of the century is a fine joke. Eighty-eight minutes of looking at people who cannot look back. What holds it is attention rather than suspense: the sense that a frame stared at long enough starts giving up information it never agreed to carry.

His wife dies; her sister stays on in the house, and what he begins to feel has nowhere to go. Miguel Picazo sets that in a Spanish household of 1964, where the arrangement is respectable exactly because it goes unspoken: a widower, an unmarried sister-in-law, a domestic order that can be defended to anyone who asks and altered by no one. The pressure is not dramatic in the usual sense. It is the pressure of rooms and meals and other people's expectations, which is why a hundred and three minutes of ordinary weeks can start to feel like a term being served. Spain put the film forward to the Academy Awards, a public gesture toward a story built on what is never said aloud in it, and the title keeps attention where it belongs: on the woman the whole household is arranged around.

Thirteen years absent, Pedro turns up at a house that is already short of money. His brother Fito drives a truck, has trouble at work and a poker habit; Juana, Fito's wife, is the one keeping the arithmetic upright. Enrique Urbizu takes two hours and seven minutes over this, a long stretch for three people in a small situation, and the length does the work: debts accumulate slowly, marriages wear through slowly, and a brother gone that long has to be absorbed rather than confronted. Nothing in the setup is exotic. A wage under pressure, a habit that eats it, a man in the doorway who used to belong there — the film sets them down in the same rooms and holds the temperature just under boiling for as long as the situation allows.

Tasio makes charcoal in rural Navarre, and the film treats that work as a life rather than a backdrop. Montxo Armendáriz follows him from boyhood through his love affairs into the ordinary middle of things, which sounds like a chronicle and plays more like a cycle of seasons: the same trade, the same country, a man who keeps choosing both while the years pile up. Ninety-five minutes, and no crisis imported from elsewhere to give the story a shape it does not need. The comedy sits in the courting and the company; the weight sits in repetition, in a job done the same way often enough to become a trait of character. It is a portrait of staying put, filmed without any argument about whether staying was the wise choice.

Eighteen minutes, one museum, and two long-dead sculptors treated as though their work could be touched. José Val del Omar filmed inside the Valladolid National Museum, among figures by Alonso de Berruguete and Juan de Juni, and called what he was after tactile vision: a phrase that sounds like a manifesto and turns out to be a plain description of method. Carved wood is taken as surface and edge before it is taken as subject. Documentary is the label, though what gets documented is a way of seeing rather than a collection. Caimán's hundred best Spanish films makes room for it at eighteen minutes, among features. The date is 1960, and the ambition still reads as ambition — to get a camera to do the work of a hand, on objects whose entire meaning lies in their relief.

Success in the opera house turns out to be the start of the difficulty rather than the end of it. Xie Jin follows Chunhua and Yuehong Xing up through the ranks of Chinese opera, and the climbing is the straightforward part; what waits at the top is a set of pressures, personal first and then social, that the stage gave neither of them any preparation for. The Golden Horse survey of the hundred greatest Chinese-language films carries it. Made in 1964 and set before the revolution, the film watches that earlier world from the far side of the change, which puts a frame around every curtain call. A hundred and twelve minutes go to two temperaments rather than one plot, and the interest is in how differently two people can read the same success.

There is a mother at home who cannot be left alone, and a shop wage that has to cover them both. Manuel Mur Oti builds Cielo negro on that arithmetic and then introduces a bohemian, who in a melodrama of 1951 is less a romance than an expense the household cannot carry. The real subject is the cost of a day: hours sold behind a counter, hours owed at a bedside, the small remainder that belongs to the woman herself. Melodrama gets accused of exaggeration, but the exaggeration here is structural rather than emotional — the situation is squeezed until its terms show, and the terms are wages, duty and time. Ninety-three minutes, and the accounting never softens, which is what gives an ordinary romance the pressure of a verdict.

Granada, filmed by a man who was born in it and never treats it as scenery. José Val del Omar gives his hometown twenty-one minutes arranged the way music is arranged: no story to follow, a rhythm to keep up with, more interest in how a place behaves than in what it contains. The word documentary sits oddly on the result, since nothing here is being established for the record. What the film wants is closer to a sensation of the city, water and all, held long enough to harden into a form. It was made in 1955, and it moves like something built for an audience that had not yet settled what cinema was for. Twenty-one minutes is also exactly the length at which such a thing stays a proposition rather than becoming a demonstration.

A letter arrives in the morning: he has agreed to fight a bull that afternoon. He is a former matador well past it, living badly with his young nephew Pepote, and the hours between the letter and the ring are the whole film. Ladislao Vajda keeps to eighty-seven minutes and gives them to practical business, a day made of errands and asking, which is the honest way to film being poor. The bullfight works as a deadline rather than a spectacle. It was put together in 1956 as an Italian production speaking Spanish, its own small piece of period logistics. The boy is the other half of the arithmetic, since whatever the afternoon costs will be paid in front of him, and the film keeps that in the room even when the talk is about nothing.

Camarón is where the film starts, not what it is about, and the difference is the whole design. Isaki Lacuesta made a documentary that keeps sliding into fiction and a fiction that keeps turning up documentary evidence, with the flamenco singer as a source of heat rather than the subject of a portrait. The conventional music film gathers testimony and archive; this one takes a song's worth of feeling and goes looking for it in living people. A hundred and nine minutes, 2006, and no announcement anywhere of which passages were arranged and which were found. The withholding is not a trick. It is the claim being made: that what a singer leaves behind is less a biography than a way of listening, and the place to look for it is somebody's ordinary afternoon.

The cutting is the argument: a family under occupation on one side, and on the other the son who left and did not stay poor. Zheng Jun-li runs it a hundred and ninety-two minutes, long enough for both halves to become habits — Sufan, the parents and the boy in one register, Zhongliang's rise through a flourishing company in the other — until the contrast stops working as a device and starts working as an accusation. Zhangmin, the brother who went into hiding to keep the family safe, is the third term nobody has room for. It was finished in 1947, with the war just behind it, and the Golden Horse survey of the hundred greatest Chinese-language films still carries it. Melodrama at this length is not indulgence; it is the only form with room to show what a separation costs in years.
